# blaze (ra-jit)

How to build, test and change ra-jit, including the vendored rust-analyzer: docs/contributing.md.
What the harnesses check: docs/harness.md. Rules live in agents/rules.ts (edit there, then `bun
agents/rules.ts --write` for AGENTS.md).

1. **no-rustc**: ra-jit never runs rustc. It compiles everything itself: no function, crate, standard
   library, build script, proc macro, check, test, doctest or link step is handed to rustc, rustdoc
   or a cargo that runs them, and there is no "fall back to cargo" path. Each place that still does
   is a bug with a `no-rustc` issue, to be removed, never extended or added to. See
   [docs/no-rustc.md](docs/no-rustc.md).
2. **no-fallback**: No fallback, ever; fail fast with a clear error. When ra-jit can't do something (an
   unsupported construct, a refused patch, a missing TypeId, a static it can't place), it stops with
   an error that names what and where, at the point it is first seen. It never quietly takes another
   path: not cargo or rustc, not rustc's copy of a function or static, not a whole build instead of
   a patch to hide a refusal, not a slower backend or an older cached result. New code adds no
   fallback. A change that touches an existing one turns it into an error in the same change, and
   where that would break a harness, fixes the bug behind it instead.
   Why: "No fallback EVER, no rustc, prefer quick error so bug can be fixed" (Andrew, 2026-10-26). A
   silent fallback hides the bug and turns it into wrong output (#386, #392); an error gets it
   fixed.
3. **superset-of-rust**: Own the whole stack, and stay a superset of Rust. Move step by step toward
   owning every layer from source to running code (front end, std, codegen, linking, loading), never
   by narrowing what ra-jit accepts: every program the pinned nightly's rustc builds
   (`harness/toolchain`) must build and behave the same under ra-jit, with the real std, C
   dependencies, build scripts and proc macros. What ra-jit adds (live edits, tiers) comes on top.
   The one allowed difference is sandboxing: build scripts and proc macros run sandboxed (#147). One
   that needs more than the sandbox allows is the only exception, and is made to work rather than
   refused where possible. See [docs/no-rustc.md](docs/no-rustc.md).
   Why: Owning every layer is what makes ra-jit fast. Sandboxing has been on by default since
   2026-10-26 (https://github.com/indexable-inc/blaze/issues/147).
4. **own-nightly**: blaze is its own toolchain: build every project with blaze's own pinned nightly
   (`harness/toolchain`), named and versioned as blaze's, whatever the project pins. Don't follow
   the project's toolchain, support stable or several rustc versions, or pin stable. The nightly
   moves only when blaze moves it, deliberately, with the corpus difftest as the gate. It is the
   language and std definition blaze matches while rustc is still in the tree, not a dependency to
   track; every rustc use left is removed on the way to none. Users keep their own toolchain and CI
   as the final word: blaze says so rather than switching toolchains. See
   [docs/no-rustc.md](docs/no-rustc.md).
   Why: "You should use your own nightly that you control since you are trying to replace rustc"
   (Andrew, 2026-10-26). We are moving off rustc entirely ("no rustc", Andrew).
5. **sandbox-everything**: Every test, build script and proc macro runs in a sandbox, by default, on
   every platform. `cargo ra-jit test` runs each test executable in one sandbox (Linux namespaces
   and seccomp, macOS Seatbelt and the interposer) under `all` and `affected` alike; every build
   script, cargo's runs and the daemon's, runs in the same one through `cargo/script_sandbox.rs`
   (writing only its `OUT_DIR`), and every proc-macro server is started in it (`macro_sandbox.rs`).
   Where none can be made it stops, rather than run outside. The only ways out are a package's
   `[package.metadata.blaze.sandbox]` (`tests = false`, `unsandboxed-tests`, `build-script =
   false`), the root manifest's `[workspace.metadata.blaze.sandbox]` (`unsandboxed-build-scripts`,
   `unsandboxed-proc-macros`) and `RA_JIT_SANDBOX=off`, never a silent fallback. Nothing new that
   runs user code runs outside it by default. See
   [docs/cargo.md#build-scripts-and-proc-macros-run-in-a-sandbox](docs/cargo.md#build-scripts-and-proc-macros-run-in-a-sandbox).
   Why: "Everything should by default be in sandbox and yea it should have sandbox support macos"
   (Andrew, 2026-10-26).
6. **best-long-term-design**: Pick the best long-term design, not the least work: own the layer,
   rewrite it or port rustc's rule properly, rather than do the least work or what a small team
   could maintain. Spend the effort on proving it right (differential tests against rustc, fuzzing,
   real crates). See [docs/contributing.md#rules-for-code](docs/contributing.md#rules-for-code).
   Why: Agents write most of ra-jit, so the amount of code a design takes is not what limits it; what
   stays expensive is proving it right.
7. **semantics-in-rust-analyzer**: Language semantics go in the rust-analyzer subtree: MIR building and
   passes, borrow checking, const eval, layout and code-identity hashes as salsa queries (what rustc
   keeps in `rustc_middle`, `rustc_mir_transform`, `rustc_borrowck`) go in `vendor/rust-analyzer`,
   as a new crate there rather than edits to upstream's files where possible. Codegen backends,
   object writing, the splice, the daemon, cargo integration, the store, tiers, the live runtime and
   the harnesses stay in `crates/`. See
   [docs/contributing.md#where-new-code-goes](docs/contributing.md#where-new-code-goes).
8. **no-mcp**: No MCP. Agent-facing interfaces are a Unix socket (local) or HTTP (remote) with one
   documented, versioned schema in deterministic CBOR (JSON only as a rendering for people), and the
   CLI is a client of the same API. See
   [docs/roadmap.md#8-the-agent-api](docs/roadmap.md#8-the-agent-api).
   Why: MCP is cringe and outdated.
9. **heavy-work-on-dev-host**: Heavy work runs on a dev host, the Mac does quick checks. Release
   builds, harness sweeps and benchmarks run on an AWS dev host claimed in the host ledger
   (`fleet-ops` skill), with a lease as long as the run, released after. See
   [docs/contributing.md#working-in-parallel](docs/contributing.md#working-in-parallel).
10. **worktree-per-lane**: One worktree per lane, never `git stash`: a uniquely named worktree with its
    own `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` or a shared sccache. Harnesses run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=0`.
    Why: The stash is shared by every worktree.
11. **land-through-queue**: Land small and often, through the merge queue only. After the local gate,
    run `python3 .github/scripts/land.py "what the branch does"` in the lane's worktree: it opens
    the pull request, waits for its run (the merge gate: the build and the unit tests, about 5
    minutes), queues it and waits until the gate has passed on it merged onto main and it is merged,
    or says why not. Every harness runs after the merge, in the release train (train.yaml), whose
    issue "Release train is red" names the commits since it was last green. Its waiting survives a
    tool that kills it; `land.py --wait` picks it up again. Never push to main or merge into it by
    hand. See [docs/contributing.md#landing-a-change](docs/contributing.md#landing-a-change).
12. **clean-up-lane**: Delete what a lane made when it is done: its worktree, target directory and
    dev-host directories, and its merged branch.
13. **credit-people**: Credit people. A commit or pull request built on someone's suggestion, diagnosis,
    workaround or patch from an issue, review or discussion gets a `Co-authored-by: Name
    <id+login@users.noreply.github.com>` trailer for each of them, and names where it came from. See
    [docs/contributing.md#credit](docs/contributing.md#credit).
14. **narration-is-a-script**: The site's narration is a podcast script, not the article read aloud.
    Each page in `site/content/` has its own spoken version, written for the ear: an `Intro`, one
    `Say` per top-level Section or Issue (a `Say` on a container replaces its whole subtree; a long
    section splits into `Say`s on its sub-blocks, the rest `Silent`) and an `Outro`. Talk to the
    listener, say why before what, describe code by what it shows and never read symbols out, keep
    each `Say` under about 90 seconds, and steer the voice with Fish Audio Drama 3 directions
    (`[warm]`, `[curious]`, `[pause]`, `[laughs]`, `<emphasis>...</emphasis>`). It must stay
    accurate to the article: a change to a page changes its script in the same commit.
    Pronunciations go in `site/audio/lexicon.toml`, which never touches text inside `[ ]`. See
    [site/audio/README.md](site/audio/README.md).
